Here are the defects I found in `top_scores`:

**1. Mutable default argument (`seen=[]`)**
The default list is created once, at function-definition time, and shared across every call that doesn't pass its own `seen`. Since the function also does `seen.append(...)` inside the loop, that shared list keeps growing permanently. Effect: a later call (with the default `seen`) will silently treat scores added to `result` by an *earlier, unrelated* call as "already seen" and exclude them — so `top_scores` can return different, incomplete results for the same input `scores` depending on call history, with no way for the caller to know why.

**2. `IndexError` when `limit` exceeds the length of `scores`**
`range(0, limit)` iterates fixed indices `0..limit-1` regardless of how many elements `scores` actually has. If `scores` has fewer than `limit` elements (e.g. 3 scores with the default `limit=5`), `scores[i]` raises `IndexError: list index out of range` instead of just returning all available scores.

**3. `ZeroDivisionError` on empty input**
`average = sum(scores) / len(scores)` divides by `len(scores)`. If `scores` is `[]` and `limit=0` (so the loop body never runs and defect #2 isn't triggered first), this raises `ZeroDivisionError`. (With `limit>0` and empty `scores`, defect #2's `IndexError` fires before this line is ever reached.)

**4. Duplicate values are dropped instead of being replaced by the next-lowest score**
The loop only ever looks at sorted indices `0..limit-1` — it never advances past `limit-1` to compensate for entries skipped by the `seen` check. So if the top `limit` sorted slots contain repeated values, those repeats are filtered out by `seen` but nothing from further down the list fills in for them. Example: `scores=[10,10,10,10,10,9,8]`, `limit=5` → `result` comes back as just `[10]`, even though `9` and `8` exist and there's no reason they shouldn't be considered — so `result` ends up with far fewer than `limit` entries even though enough distinct scores exist in `scores`.

**5. In-place sort mutates the caller's list**
`scores.sort(reverse=True)` reorders the list object the caller passed in, as a side effect, rather than sorting a copy. Any other code holding a reference to that same list (or depending on its original ordering) will see it permanently changed after calling `top_scores`.
